act.name: Discover
act.tagline: What's really there — and can we build it?

title: Investigate the Real Problem
goal: Find out, with evidence, what actually goes wrong in the system, how much, and why.

processes.title: Investigate the Real Problem
processes.summary: Reproduce and trace today's flow, measure the baseline, find the root causes and write the technical problem statement.

definition.purpose: Find out, with evidence, what actually goes wrong in the system, how much, and why.
definition.outcome: A technical problem statement backed by a reproduced trace, a measured baseline and evidenced root causes.
definition.jtbd: When the problem is framed, help me see it happen, measure it and find its causes, so the solution hits the real thing.

normal: Reproduce & trace the current flow
Measure the baseline
Find the root causes
Write the technical problem statement
parallel: Baseline queries run while the trace is finished
Spikes from the plan can start in parallel

cases.happyPath: The problem reproduces, logs give clean numbers and two or three causes explain most of it.
alternates: Manual process → time-and-motion instead of logs
No logs → timed samples with wider ranges

routing.forward: Technical problem statement → 1.4 Research Solution Options
routing.alternate: Obvious problem → short trace and baseline
routing.rework: Unevidenced causes → back to the trace
routing.escalation: Needs production or data access → system or data owner
routing.stop: No real problem in the numbers → back to framing or stop — recorded in the learning log

checks: Tech lead reviews method and statement

concerns: Fixing a story instead of the problem
decisions: Is this the problem we'll solve?

execution.authority: Tech lead accepts the statement; system and data owners grant read access.

continuity.handoff: Technical problem statement with trace, baseline and root causes → 1.4 Research Solution Options
traceability: Creates RC-## and TPS-##; every clause links to trace steps and baselines
measures: Share of statement clauses with measured evidence
learning: How far the problem moved from the brief — learning log

loops: Cause not visible in the trace

lessons.title: Reproduce & Trace the Current Flow
lessons.summary: Make the problem happen on demand and trace it step by step through the systems.

definition.purpose: See the problem happen with your own eyes, in a safe environment, and know exactly where in the flow it happens.
definition.outcome: A step-by-step trace of today's flow with timings, systems and manual steps, reproducible by someone else.
definition.jtbd: Help me see the problem happen, so I'm not fixing a story about it.
exit: Problem reproduced in a test environment or on real samples

normal: Pick real samples or a recorded case
Reproduce the flow in a test environment
Trace each step: system, timing, data, manual work
Mark where it goes wrong
Hand the trace to someone else to repeat

cases.happyPath: The problem reproduces on the first sample set and the trace is clear.
alternates: Problem only appears under load → reproduce with a scripted batch
edgeCases: Intermittent failure → collect several runs and their logs
exceptions: No test environment → observe the real flow read-only and record it
failures: The problem can't be reproduced at all

routing.alternate: Manual flow → time-and-motion trace instead of logs
routing.rework: Not repeatable → trace again with more detail
routing.escalation: Needs production access → tech lead and system owner
routing.stop: Can't be reproduced → back to framing with what you saw — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Every step has system, timing and data
policies: Real samples are masked before use

concerns: Fixing a problem nobody has seen
decisions: Where exactly does it go wrong?

agents: AI coding agent for reading logs

continuity.handoff: Current flow trace → 1.3.2 Measure the Baseline
traceability: Trace steps link to DF-## and SYS-##
learning: Where the real flow differed from the map — learning log

workflows.title: Trace the Flow
workflows.summary: Reproduce today's flow on real, masked samples in a safe environment and trace every step with its system, timing, data and manual work.

steps.title: Pick real samples to reproduce with
steps.ask: Help me pick a small, representative set of real samples to reproduce with (normal, edge and failing cases), and tell me exactly what to mask before using them.

steps.title: Reproduce the flow safely
steps.ask: Give me step-by-step instructions to reproduce today's flow in our test environment with those samples, including what to log or time at each step.

steps.title: Trace each step with timings
steps.ask: Turn my notes and logs into flow-trace rows: step, what happens, system (SYS ID), data in → out, manual or not, median time, and whether it goes wrong there.

lenses.note: Data in and out at every step.
Which system each step runs on.

steps.title: Reproduced reliably?
steps.ask: Check my trace could be repeated by another engineer from what's written, and list anything missing.

contract.definition: Reproduce today's flow on real, masked samples in a safe environment and trace every step with its system, timing, data and manual work.
criteria: System, timing and data per step
contract.handoff: Current flow trace → 1.3.2 Measure the Baseline
traceability: Each trace step links to DF-## and SYS-##
learning: Where the real flow differed from the map — learning log

objectives: Reproduce the problem safely on masked samples
Trace each step with system, data and time
lessons.exercise: Trace the four steps of handling one order, with system, data and median time for each. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: You can't reproduce the problem. What next?
options: Fix what you think it is
Go back to framing with what you did see
quiz.why: No reproduction, no fix — reframe with the evidence you have.

lessons.prompt:
I'm working through "Reproduce & Trace the Current Flow" (Discover → Investigate the Real Problem) on my own project. Act as my assistant: draft and check, I decide.

Goal: See the problem happen with your own eyes, in a safe environment, and know exactly where in the flow it happens.
Done looks like: A step-by-step trace of today's flow with timings, systems and manual steps, reproducible by someone else.

I'll attach or paste: Technical framing pack; Data flow map; Repository & environment access.

Work through these steps with me, one at a time:
1. Pick real samples to reproduce with → Current flow trace
   Help me pick a small, representative set of real samples to reproduce with (normal, edge and failing cases), and tell me exactly what to mask before using them.
2. Reproduce the flow safely → Current flow trace
   Give me step-by-step instructions to reproduce today's flow in our test environment with those samples, including what to log or time at each step.
3. Trace each step with timings → Current flow trace
   Turn my notes and logs into flow-trace rows: step, what happens, system (SYS ID), data in → out, manual or not, median time, and whether it goes wrong there.
4. Reproduced reliably? (a decision — give me the options and a recommendation; I make the call)
   Check my trace could be repeated by another engineer from what's written, and list anything missing.

Produce: Current flow trace. Use clear headings I can paste into my document.

Before you finish, check it against: Every step has system, timing and data; Manual steps marked; System, timing and data per step; Repeatable.

Ask me for anything you need instead of guessing. Keep it specific to my project.

lessons.title: Measure the Baseline
lessons.summary: Measure today's performance, errors and volumes so every option can be judged against real numbers.

definition.purpose: Replace estimates with measurements, so the problem and every option are judged against today's real numbers.
definition.outcome: Baseline measurements for each success metric: method, sample, median, p95 and source — reusable later.
definition.jtbd: Help me know how bad it really is today, in numbers I can defend.
exit: Every success metric has a measured baseline
Method written so it can be re-run

normal: Pick the metrics from the success metrics
Choose the source: logs, database, timings
Pull a representative sample
Compute median, p95 and error rates
Record the method

cases.happyPath: Logs give two weeks of clean data for every metric.
alternates: No logs → time a sample by hand and say so
edgeCases: Seasonal volumes → measure peak and normal separately
exceptions: Data is partial → state coverage and confidence

routing.forward: Baseline measurements → 1.3.3 Find the Root Causes
routing.alternate: Manual timings only → wider confidence range
routing.stop: Baseline shows no real problem → back to framing — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Every number has a method, sample size and period
Medians and percentiles, not averages alone

agents: AI coding agent for writing queries
execution.authority: Tech lead accepts the baseline; the data owner grants read access.

continuity.handoff: Baseline measurements → 1.3.3 Find the Root Causes
learning: Metrics that were hard to measure — learning log

workflows.title: Measure the Baseline
workflows.summary: Measure today's numbers for every success metric from logs, data or timings, with a method another engineer could re-run.

steps.title: Pick metrics & data sources
steps.ask: For each success metric, tell me the best data source (logs, database, timed sample) and write the exact query or method to measure it.

lenses.note: Measure what the user waits for.

steps.title: Pull a representative sample
steps.ask: Help me choose a representative period and sample — covering normal and peak load — and say what would make it unrepresentative.

lenses.note: A representative period — normal and peak.

steps.title: Compute medians, p95 & error rates
steps.ask: From the raw results I paste, compute median, p95 and error rates per metric, and fill the baseline rows with method, period, sample and confidence.

lenses.note: Median and p95, not averages alone.
Use existing logs before building new probes.

steps.title: Baseline trustworthy?
steps.ask: Check my baseline method for bias or gaps before the tech lead reviews it.

loops: No real problem in the numbers

contract.definition: Measure today's numbers for every success metric from logs, data or timings, with a method another engineer could re-run.
criteria: Method, sample and period per number
contract.handoff: Baseline measurements → 1.3.3 Find the Root Causes
learning: Metrics that were hard to measure — learning log

objectives: Measure today's numbers with a re-runnable method
lessons.exercise: Write the query or method for 'orders lost or duplicated' and the period you'd use. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: Your sample is from the quietest week of the year. Is it a good baseline?
options: No — cover normal and peak, or say it's unrepresentative
quiz.why: A baseline must represent the load the solution will face.

lessons.title: Find the Root Causes
lessons.summary: Trace the symptoms down to the technical causes, each backed by evidence.

definition.purpose: Fix causes, not symptoms: find what in the system produces the problem, with evidence for each cause.
definition.outcome: A root-cause analysis: symptoms, why-chains, contributing causes by category, and the evidence for each.
definition.jtbd: Help me find what actually causes this, so the solution hits the cause.
exit: Every cause backed by trace or measurement evidence

normal: List the symptoms from the trace and baseline
Run why-chains on each
Sort causes by category: data, integration, code, infrastructure, manual step
Check each cause against evidence
Rank by contribution
parallel: Why-chains run per symptom in parallel

cases.happyPath: Two or three causes explain most of the baseline.
alternates: One cause dominates → still check for contributing ones
edgeCases: Cause sits in a vendor system → record it as a constraint

routing.forward: Root causes → 1.3.4 Write the Technical Problem Statement
routing.rework: Unevidenced causes → back to the trace
routing.escalation: Cause in a system we can't change → tech lead and owner
routing.stop: Cause is non-technical (training, policy) → stop and hand it back to the client — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Each cause cites trace or measurement evidence
rules: Blame the system, not the person
policies: Causes are stated without naming individuals

agents: AI coding agent for clustering symptoms

continuity.handoff: Technical root-cause analysis → 1.3.4 Write the Technical Problem Statement
traceability: Creates RC-## linked to trace steps and baselines
learning: Causes that surprised the team — learning log

workflows.title: Find the Causes
workflows.summary: Take each symptom from the trace and baseline down a why-chain to its technical cause, and keep only the causes the evidence supports.

steps.title: List the symptoms
steps.ask: From my trace and baseline, list the symptoms, each with its number.

steps.title: Run why-chains on each
steps.ask: For each symptom, build a why-chain down to a system condition — data, integration, code, infrastructure or a manual step — never a person.

lenses.note: Stop at a system condition, not a person.

steps.title: Check each cause against evidence
steps.ask: For each cause, find the evidence in my trace, baseline or logs, mark any cause without evidence, and rank the causes by how much of the baseline they explain.

steps.title: Causes evidenced?
steps.ask: Challenge my root causes: which are symptoms in disguise, and which lack evidence?

lenses.note: Do the causes explain most of the baseline?

loops: Cause in a system we can't change

contract.definition: Take each symptom from the trace and baseline down a why-chain to its technical cause, and keep only the causes the evidence supports.
decisions: Is every cause backed by evidence?
recovery: Ask why again until a system or data cause appears
Rewrite as the condition that let it happen
contract.rework: Unevidenced causes → back to the trace
contract.handoff: Technical root-cause analysis → 1.3.4 Write the Technical Problem Statement
traceability: RC-## links to trace steps and baselines
learning: Causes that surprised the team — learning log

objectives: Keep only causes the evidence supports
lessons.exercise: Run a why-chain on '3.1% of order lines are wrong'. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: A cause has no evidence. What do you do?
options: Go back to the trace or mark it unproven
quiz.why: Unevidenced causes send the solution the wrong way.

lessons.title: Write the Technical Problem Statement
lessons.summary: One statement of the problem in the system: what fails, how much, why, and within which limits.

definition.purpose: Bring the evidence into one technical problem statement every option will be judged against.
definition.outcome: A technical problem statement: what fails, where, how much (baseline), why (causes), within which constraints, and what a solution must achieve.
definition.jtbd: Help me state the problem so clearly that the right solution becomes obvious and the wrong ones rule themselves out.
exit: Statement accepted by the tech lead

normal: Draft the statement from the template
Link every clause to its evidence
Check it has no solution words
Read it back to the tech lead

cases.happyPath: One clear statement, every clause linked.
alternates: Two separate problems emerge → one statement each, ranked
edgeCases: Problem is smaller than the brief suggested → say so plainly
exceptions: Problem bigger than the brief → flag scope to the tech lead
failures: The statement can't be supported by the evidence

routing.forward: Technical problem statement → 1.4 Research Solution Options
routing.escalation: Scope differs from the brief → tech lead and client
routing.stop: No problem worth solving technically → stop and record why — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Every clause links to a trace, baseline or cause
Targets from the success metrics included
rules: A clause without evidence is removed or marked an assumption

principles: Fall in love with the problem

concerns: A problem statement that smuggles in a solution
decisions: Is this the problem we'll solve?

agents: AI coding agent for checking traceability
execution.authority: Tech lead accepts the statement; the client is told if scope changed.

continuity.handoff: Technical problem statement → 1.4 Research Solution Options
traceability: Creates TPS-## whose clauses link RC-##, baselines and C-##
learning: How far the problem moved from the brief — learning log

knowledge.Fall in love with the problem: Fall in love with the problem

workflows.title: State the Problem
workflows.summary: Write one technical problem statement from the evidence — what fails, how much, why, within which limits, and what success looks like — with every clause linked.

steps.title: Draft the statement
steps.ask: Draft the technical problem statement in five parts: what fails and where, how much (baseline), why (root causes), within which limits (hard constraints), and what a solution must achieve (targets). No technology named.

lenses.note: What fails, where, how much, why, within which limits.

steps.title: Link every clause to evidence
steps.ask: Link every clause to its evidence — trace step, baseline row, RC or C ID — and mark any clause you can't link.

steps.title: Strip out solution words
steps.ask: Read the statement for solution words, vague words ('slow', 'better') and unsupported claims, and rewrite them.

uses.name: Fall in love with the problem
uses.ref: Fall in love with the problem

steps.title: Statement accepted?
steps.ask: Prepare the statement for the tech lead's read-back, with the evidence links listed underneath.

lenses.note: Could this statement rule out a bad option?

contract.definition: Write one technical problem statement from the evidence — what fails, how much, why, within which limits, and what success looks like — with every clause linked.
decisions: Does the tech lead accept the statement?
recovery: Rewrite in terms of behaviour and numbers
contract.handoff: Technical problem statement → 1.4 Research Solution Options
traceability: TPS-## clauses link to RC-##, baselines and C-##
learning: How far the problem moved from the brief — learning log

objectives: Write one traced technical problem statement
lessons.exercise: Write TPS-01 for the order-intake case in five clauses: what fails, how much, why, limits, a solution must…. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: A clause names a technology. What now?
options: Rewrite it as behaviour and numbers
quiz.why: The statement must rule options in or out, not pick one.
